phonemes.desc: Long back-mid rounded vowel [oː]; the macron marks length only. The exact quality varies by dialect (Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet, Ugaritic mt is vowelless in writing).

pronunciation.approximation: 'MOHT' — one syllable with a long, drawn-out o (or oo) and a crisp final t.

pronunciation.note: The name is the Canaanite word for 'death.' The macron on the registrable Mōt signals vowel length, not a fixed quality: Phoenician has mūt, Hebrew māwet, and Ugaritic mt gives no vowels. We follow the PUNICODEX macron convention with /moːt/; hear a long low/back vowel rather than the short English 'o.' Tier 1: the macron preserves a reconstructed long vowel. Sources: KTU, CIS/KAI, Smith The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Day Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan.

domains.title: The Devouring King
domains.subtitle: Death, Drought, and the Underworld
domains.lead: Mōt is the personified appetite of death in Canaanite myth — not a reaper with a scythe but a being whose throat is a chasm and whose jaws grind gods and mortals alike. In the Baꜥal Cycle he is the necessary opposite of the storm-god: where Baꜥal brings rain, Mōt brings the parched season when growth stops and the world turns to dust.

cards.name: Personified Death
cards.desc: The name itself is the Canaanite word for death; in Ugaritic he is a god, not merely an abstraction.

cards.name: Insatiable Hunger
cards.desc: KTU 1.5 i describes a throat like a lion's, a gullet like a whale's, and an appetite that swallows armies.

cards.name: Seasonal Drought
cards.desc: His victory over Baꜥal brings years of barrenness; his defeat restores the rains and the fertility of the land.

cards.name: Underworld Sovereign
cards.desc: He rules the arṣ, the land of death to which every living thing must eventually descend.

symbols.name: Devouring mouth
symbols.meaning: His throat is the abyss — 'like a whale's gullet' (KTU 1.5 i) — that swallows Baꜥal whole

symbols.name: Dust and dry earth
symbols.meaning: The landscape of his kingdom; when he wins, the world becomes his emblem

symbols.name: Sword and winnowing fan
symbols.meaning: The harvest tools ꜥAnat turns against him (KTU 1.6 ii)

symbols.name: Seven portions
symbols.meaning: The meal he demands — meat by double handfuls, drink by the riverful (KTU 1.4 viii)

symbols.name: Desert wasteland
symbols.meaning: The parched country that announces his season has begun

mythology.lead: Mōt's mythology is the dark season of the year made personal. His stories are preserved in the Baꜥal Cycle, where he confronts Baꜥal, kills him, and is in turn destroyed and reborn in a cycle that explains drought, death, and the return of fertility.

myths.title: The Appetite of Death
myths.text: Death in the Canaanite imagination is not a reaper but an eater. When Baꜥal finishes his cedar palace and hosts the gods at his banquet, Mōt sends an answer from the underworld: because he was not invited, he will feast — and his dish is Baꜥal himself (KTU 1.4 vii–viii). His messengers describe their master with a connoisseur's precision: a throat like a lion's, a gullet like a whale's, 'a lip to the earth, a lip to the heavens... by double handfuls he eats, by the riverful he drinks.' The divine assembly is warned not to approach him too closely, 'lest he make you like a lamb in his mouth' (KTU 1.4 viii 17–20). The horror of the portrait is its honesty: Mōt does not hate; he hungers, without malice and without limit. He is the one guest who cannot be excluded forever, and the banquet of the gods is real only because he has agreed, for now, to wait.

myths.title: The Storm God in the Mouth of Mot
myths.text: Baꜥal does what no storm should: he goes down. Taking his clouds, winds, and bolts with him, he descends into Mōt's realm of dust, grime, and drought, 'into the throat of Death, son of El' (KTU 1.5). On earth the consequences are immediate. Ēl mourns like a mortal, sitting in the dust and gashing himself with a stone knife; Asherah orders the rites of mourning; ꜥAnat ranges the world searching. For seven years — the dry season made calendar — the rain withholds, the fields fail, and even the gods grow thin. The narrative power of the scene lies in its refusal of rescue: the high god cannot simply decree Baꜥal back, because Mōt's claim is legitimate within the order of things. Death, in this theology, is not a rebellion against creation but one of its standing institutions — the shadow the feast casts, the price the rains will eventually have to pay.

myths.title: Anat Grinds Death Like Grain
myths.text: The answer to Death comes not from heaven's throne but from a sister's rage. After burying Baꜥal on Zaphon, ꜥAnat seizes Mōt and subjects him to the full grammar of the harvest he has starved (KTU 1.6 ii 30–35): 'with a sword she splits him, with a sieve she winnows him, with fire she burns him, with millstones she grinds him, in a field she scatters him.' The sequence is agricultural to the last verb — this is threshing, sifting, milling, and sowing — so that the destruction of death itself is imagined as the processing of grain. Scholars have long noted the deep logic: you cannot kill death, but you can reduce it, distribute it, return it to the soil as something the living can use. Baꜥal comes back by the word of El, and the rains return. The myth's consolation is not that death is defeated once for all, but that death, ground fine enough, becomes compost.

myths.title: Seven Years Later
myths.text: Mōt does not stay scattered. Seven years after his threshing he returns and finds Baꜥal again (KTU 1.6 vi), and the two gods fall into elemental combat — they gore like bulls, bite like serpents, kick like stallions, neither able to prevail. The deadlock is broken not by force but by light. The sun goddess Šāpšu warns Mōt: 'How can you battle Baꜥal the Conqueror?... El will overturn your throne of kingship, he will break your staff of judgment.' Mōt, deflated, concedes the kingship and retires to his own realm for his seasons. The ending is the cycle's most sophisticated moment: death is not destroyed — the earlier threshing bought only seven years — but it is bound to its time, pushed back by a coalition of love, light, and the old god's law. Fertility is not a permanent conquest; it is an annually renewed armistice, and the world survives on the terms of that truce.

lore.syncretism: The Hellenistic Phoenician account preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea — quoting Philo of Byblos, who summarized Sanchuniathon — makes Mōt (Muth) a son of El and Rhea, deified after death and identified by the Phoenicians with the Greek Thanatos and Pluto. A more speculative cosmogonic strand in the same tradition makes Mōt arise from primal mud or putrefaction, the source from which the seeds of creation emerge. In the Hebrew Bible the common noun māwet ('death') sometimes appears almost personified, especially in Hosea 13:14, suggesting that the Canaanite figure lingered in Israelite imagination even where he was no longer worshipped.
lore.culturalLegacy: Mōt's name survives in Hebrew māwet, Arabic mawt, and the common Semitic root for death itself — the god never outlived the noun. His myth helped shape later personifications of death in biblical and apocalyptic literature, from the personified Death of Hosea 13:14 to the pale rider of Revelation, and the Baꜥal–Mōt cycle has long fascinated scholars as a Near Eastern parallel to — and a warning against facile equations with — later dying-and-rising god traditions. Philo of Byblos, as quoted by Eusebius, still remembered a Phoenician Muth whom the learned identified with the Greek Thanatos and Pluto. In modern fantasy, games, and Neopagan reconstructions, Mōt appears as the Canaanite lord of the underworld, gaunt and voracious. He endures as the figure every pantheon must make room for: the one who says, without anger, that all feasting ends here.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Mōt is the god nobody wants to meet and nobody can avoid. He is not evil; he is hungry. His throat does not distinguish between good and bad, rich and poor, god and mortal. That is what makes him terrifying, and that is what makes him honest. Every other deity in the pantheon has favorites; Mōt has only appetite.

Yet Mōt is also necessary. Without the dry season, the seed would rot. Without the limit of death, life would have no shape. The Canaanites did not deny him; they told stories about how to survive him — how a sister's rage, a sun-goddess's warning, and a storm's return could push death back into its season. Mōt teaches that mortality is not a punishment but a boundary, and that the boundary is what makes the feast possible.

lore.archaeology: The Baꜥal Cycle tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.4–1.6) are the principal witnesses to Mōt's mythology, preserving his threats, his swallowing of Baꜥal, and his dismemberment by ꜥAnat in alphabetic cuneiform. The Hellenistic Phoenician cosmogony survives only in the excerpts of Philo of Byblos transmitted by Eusebius. No distinct sanctuary of Mōt has been identified, but the widespread West Semitic word for death — Ugaritic mt, Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet, Akkadian mūtu — testifies to the concept's deep cultural reach.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎎𐎚 (m-t), Phoenician 𐤌𐤕 (m-t), and Hebrew מות (m-w-t). The macron over ō in Mōt marks a reconstructed long vowel; the actual quality differs by dialect (Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet), while Ugaritic mt is vowelless in writing. The name is the common Canaanite word for 'death,' here personified as a god. Tier 1: the macron preserves a reconstructed long vowel.
